'''Thanasis Economou''' (born 6 May 1937) is a [[Greeks|Greek]] [[Nuclear physics|nuclear physicist]] and scientist associated with the [[University of Chicago]]'s [[Enrico Fermi Institute]]. He has developed scientific instruments for interplanetary spacecraft since the mid-1960s and has participated in a number of [[NASA]] and other planetary missions. He was one of the scientists who designed and built the [[Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer]] (APXS) used by the [[Mars Pathfinder]] mission in 1997.<ref name=":0">{{cite news |last=Koppes |first=Steve |title=From Mars to asteroids |work=University of Chicago Chronicle |date=4 February 1999 |url=https://chronicle.uchicago.edu/990204/economou.shtml |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |title=Rock-solid success for U of C Mars device |magazine=University of Chicago Magazine |date=August 1997 |url=https://magazine.uchicago.edu/9708/9708JournalMars.html |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Economou was born in 1937 in the village of [[Ziakas, Grevena|Ziakas]], in the [[Grevena (regional unit)|Grevena]] region of northern Greece. He began his schooling at the age of 11 and later studied nuclear physics at [[Charles University]] in [[Prague]]. According to the [[Hellenic Astronomical Society]], he received an M.S. in Nuclear Physics in 1961 and a postgraduate degree in 1964.<ref>{{cite web |title=Economou Thanasis |website=Hellenic Astronomical Society |url=https://helas.gr/phdslist.php?ch=E |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite web |title=Dr. Thanasis Economou |website=PanHellenic Scholarship Foundation |url=https://www.panhellenicsf.org/dr-thanasis-economou |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref>

In 1964, Economou moved to the [[United States]] and joined the Laboratory for Astrophysics and Space Research at the [[University of Chicago]]. He subsequently became associated with the university's Enrico Fermi Institute, where he worked on scientific instrumentation for space exploration.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Individual Listing: Thanasis Economou |website=University of Chicago Directory |url=https://directory.uchicago.edu/individuals/714 |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref>

== Scientific work ==

=== Lunar missions ===

During the 1960s, Economou worked with a research group led by physicist [[Anthony L. Turkevich|Anthony Turkevich]] on instruments using [[Alpha particle|alpha-particle]] backscattering to determine the chemical composition of planetary surfaces. The instruments were used on NASA's [[Surveyor program|Surveyor]] lunar missions, including Surveyor 5, 6 and 7, which landed on the Moon in 1967 and 1968.<ref name=":2">{{cite web |title=Thanasis Economou |website=The Planetary Society |url=https://www.planetary.org/profiles/thanasis-economou |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref><ref name="applicationofradioactive">{{cite journal |last=Economou |first=Thanasis E. |title=Application of radioactive sources in analytical instruments for planetary exploration |journal=Applied Radiation and Isotopes |volume=68 |issue=4–5 |pages=542–545 |year=2010 |doi=10.1016/j.apradiso.2009.09.011 |pmid=19850487}}</ref> The instruments developed for the Surveyor missions formed the basis for later instruments developed by Economou and his collaborators for planetary exploration.<ref name=":3">{{cite news |title=Life on Mars? University-created instrument may help find answer |work=University of Chicago Chronicle |date=7 November 1996 |url=https://chronicle.uchicago.edu/961107/mars.shtml |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref>

=== Mars Pathfinder ===

Economou and Anthony Turkevich designed and built the Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) carried by the [[Sojourner (rover)|Sojourner]] rover during NASA's Mars Pathfinder mission. The mission landed on Mars in July 1997. The APXS was used to determine the chemical composition of Martian rocks and soil,and performed the first chemical analysis of Martian rocks during the mission.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{cite news |title=Martian mysteries |work=University of Chicago Chronicle |date=25 September 1997 |url=https://chronicle.uchicago.edu/970925/mars.shtml |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref> The Pathfinder APXS results were subsequently reported in peer-reviewed research.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Foley |first1=Catherine Nicole |last2=Economou |first2=Thanasis E. |last3=Clayton |first3=Robert N. |title=Final chemical results from the Mars Pathfinder alpha proton X-ray spectrometer |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets |volume=108 |issue=E12 |year=2003 |doi=10.1029/2002JE002019}}</ref>

In 1998, Economou was among members of the Mars Pathfinder team and instrument developers who received the [[National Air and Space Museum]] Trophy for Current Achievement.<ref name=":0" />

=== Other planetary missions ===

Economou subsequently worked on instruments for a number of planetary and space missions. These included the [[Mars Exploration Rover]] missions, which carried APXS instruments derived from the Pathfinder instrument, as well as NASA's [[Cassini–Huygens|Cassini]] mission to [[Saturn]], the [[Stardust (spacecraft)|Stardust]] mission to comet [[81P/Wild]], and the [[Rosetta (spacecraft)|Rosetta]] mission to comet [[67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko]].<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite news |last=Koppes |first=Steve |title=Space flight instruments headed to Mars, Saturn to detect rock, soil composition |work=University of Chicago Chronicle |date=17 April 2003 |url=https://chronicle.uchicago.edu/030417/spaceflight.shtml |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref> Economou also participated in the Stardust mission, which carried a dust flux monitor instrument developed by researchers at the University of Chicago. The spacecraft encountered comet Wild 2 in 2004 and was subsequently redirected for the Stardust-NExT mission to comet [[9P/Tempel]].<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite magazine |title=Space time |magazine=University of Chicago Magazine |url=https://mag.uchicago.edu/science-medicine/space-time |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref>

He has published research on the use of radioactive sources in analytical instruments for planetary exploration.<ref name="applicationofradioactive" />

== Greek names on Mars ==

Economou proposed Greek names for several informal locations associated with the exploration of Mars by the Mars Exploration Rover missions, including [[Agrafa]] and [[Kalabaka]].<ref name=":4">{{cite news |title=Θανάσης Οικονόμου: Ο άνθρωπος που βάφτισε με ελληνικά ονόματα τον Άρη |work=[[Ta Nea]] |date=28 February 2021 |language=el |url=https://www.tanea.gr/2021/02/28/science-technology/thanasis-oikonomou-o-anthropos-pou-vaftise-me-ellinika-onomata-ton-ari/ |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref> ''[[Ta Nea]]'' referred to Economou as the "godfather of Mars" in connection with his proposals for Greek names for Martian locations.<ref name=":4" />

== Awards and recognition ==

* In 1998, Economou was among the Mars Pathfinder team members and instrument developers who received the National Air and Space Museum Trophy for Current Achievement.<ref name=":0" />
* In 2007, he received an honorary doctorate from the [[Technological Educational Institute of Western Macedonia]] in Greece.<ref name=":1" />
* In 2009, Economou received the Niki Award from Friends of Athens Information Technology for his scientific work and contributions to space exploration.<ref>{{cite web |title=Greek Scientist from NASA Receives AIT's Niki Award 2009 |website=National Documentation Centre (EKT) |date=21 December 2009 |url=https://archive.ekt.gr/content/display2167.html?prnbr=79032&ses_lang=en&ses_mode=rnd |access-date=8 August 2026}}</ref>
* In the same year, he received the Paradigm Award from the PanHellenic Scholarship Foundation, which recognized his career in planetary instrumentation and his involvement in space missions.<ref name=":1" />
